docs.title: Provider Datalab
docs.text:
Provider Datalab creates shared data workspaces on Kubernetes. A team declares its users, sessions, and services in a Datalab resource. Crossplane creates the resources from the platform's shared settings.

The platform operator installs the controllers and sets the identity, network, storage, security, quota, and backup rules. Users can then work with data through the browser or start a session with an editor and terminal.

docs.title: Create a workspace
docs.text:
After installation, apply a resource such as:

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: demo
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users:
  - alice
  sessions:
  - name: default

This creates a workspace for Alice with a persistent home directory. Educates runs its editor, terminal, and tools. Stopping the session keeps its workspace PVC; starting it again uses the same volume.

The shared Data service, packageR, gives Alice a file browser for the Datalab's object storage. When a permanent Data address is enabled, she can use it without a running session. To publish files, place them in the Datalab's public folder and send the public share link. Readers do not need an account. See Data and sharing.

docs.title: Add managed services
docs.text:
The same resource can request services for the team:

Field Service spec.databases PostgreSQL clusters and logical databases spec.documentStores MongoDB stores spec.cacheStores Redis stores spec.vectorStores Qdrant stores spec.registry A Docker registry

The cluster needs the operator for each requested managed store. The platform team manages its storage, backups, upgrades, and deletion. Provider Datalab uses an existing object-storage endpoint and credentials; it does not create buckets. Provider Storage can create those separately.

docs.title: Read the guides
docs.text:
Start with Installation to prepare the platform. Use a Datalab explains the resource fields with examples for sessions, stores, Data, and workshop content.

Authentication covers browser sign-in and Datalab roles. Security explains the other access controls. For command-line data access, use S3 client access. For services you deploy yourself, use Additional services.

The API reference lists every field. ADR-001 explains the choice of the Datalab API and Educates runtime.

docs.title: ADR-001: Use Datalab as the Public Contract
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Implemented.

Users create a Datalab. Provider Datalab turns it into a working data workspace and reports session information on the same resource.

Educates is the core runtime used by the current implementation. Its resources are created and managed internally; users and client tools do not need to know about them.

Educates also provides the browser editor and terminal.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A data workspace needs many things: an editor, a terminal, persistent files, credentials, networking, and optional services. Exposing every resource needed to build that workspace would give users a complicated and fragile API.

We need one stable contract that describes what a user wants, while allowing the implementation behind it to change.

docs.title: Make Datalab the only public workspace resource
docs.text:
Users and GitOps tools work with the namespaced Datalab resource. It describes the desired workspace, including its named sessions and optional capabilities.

The Datalab name, namespace, and UID form its stable identity. Generated Pod, Secret, and runtime-resource names are not part of the public contract.

docs.title: Use Educates as the internal runtime primitive
docs.text:
Educates provides the editor, terminal, workspace Pod, session runtime, and optional applications. Crossplane translates a Datalab into the Educates and Kubernetes resources required to run it.

This translation is an implementation detail:

User or GitOps tool
  -> Datalab
     -> Provider Datalab reconciliation
        -> internal runtime resources
           -> working Datalab session

Clients never create, update, discover, or depend on Educates resources directly. Crossplane owns those generated resources. This keeps one source of truth and lets the runtime implementation evolve without changing how users manage a Datalab.

The same rule applies if the internal runtime changes later. Runtime resources remain projections of the Datalab and do not become a second public workspace API.

docs.title: Keep user choices separate from operator policy
docs.text:
The Datalab spec contains choices that a user is allowed to make. The operator-owned EnvironmentConfig contains platform settings such as ingress, Keycloak realm, storage classes, security defaults, and extension packages.

Crossplane combines both sets of input. Users therefore get a small API, while operators keep control of security and infrastructure policy.

docs.title: Manage sessions through the Datalab
docs.text:
Each session has a unique name and a desired state such as started or stopped. Provider Datalab creates the internal runtime for started sessions and reports the observed phase, message, and browser URL in Datalab.status.sessions.

Clients read the Datalab status. They do not look up the internal runtime. Diagnostic phase and message text is not a stable machine-readable lifecycle API; richer clients will need typed status fields.

The current API does not have a separate environment or profile object. Add such concepts only through a separate decision and a compatible API change.

docs.title: Keep credentials out of the API
docs.text:
Credentials are read from referenced Kubernetes Secrets and copied only where the runtime needs them. Secret values never belong in the Datalab spec, status, logs, or normal client output.

Credentials and security settings currently apply to the whole Datalab. Use separate Datalabs when workloads need separate Kubernetes control planes or a stronger trust boundary.

docs.title: Add tools without changing the contract
docs.text: Operators can add runtime tools through extension packages. This keeps the Datalab API stable and avoids baking every tool into one large base image.

docs.title: Why This Design
docs.text: Design choice Reason One Datalab API Users have one clear object to create, review, and manage. Educates stays internal Clients are not coupled to runtime-specific resources or names. Access runtime stays internal The access implementation can change without creating a second user API. Crossplane owns generated resources Reconciliation has one owner and does not compete with user changes. User input and operator policy are separate Self-service does not bypass platform security or infrastructure rules. Status is copied to the Datalab Clients do not need broad access to internal resources. Credentials stay in Secrets The public API does not become a credential-delivery channel.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Provider Datalab is self-contained: clients need only the Datalab API.
  • Educates is essential to the current implementation but is not part of the client contract.
  • Changing the internal runtime does not require a second public workspace model.
  • Crossplane remains responsible for generated-resource ownership and cleanup.
  • Operators must validate user-selectable Secret references and other policy-sensitive options.
  • Some lifecycle behavior still needs live transition tests.

docs.title: Additional services
docs.text:
Run services such as Dask or MLflow as Kubernetes workloads from your Datalab terminal. These examples need Kubernetes API access and permission to create Pods, Deployments, Services, and PVCs in the target namespace.

Use a vCluster for tools that need their own CRDs, controllers, or cluster roles. For a short-lived process, you can run it in the terminal and use the editor's Ports tab to open its web interface.

For PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Qdrant, and a registry, first check whether the managed service fields meet your needs. The platform operator maintains those services and their backups.

docs.title: Dask
docs.text:
Dask runs tasks across a scheduler and workers. This example creates one scheduler and one worker in the current namespace. Connect to the scheduler from Python with dask.distributed.Client.

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  selector:
    app: dask-scheduler
  ports:
    - name: tcp-scheduler
      port: 8786
      targetPort: 8786
    - name: http-dashboard
      port: 8787
      targetPort: 8787
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-scheduler
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-scheduler
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scheduler
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-scheduler", "--dashboard-address", ":8787"]
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8786
            - containerPort: 8787
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-worker
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-worker", "tcp://dask-scheduler:8786", "--nthreads", "2", "--memory-limit", "2GB"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
EOF
Open the scheduler dashboard through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/dask-scheduler 8787:8787

Dask Gateway also needs cluster-wide resources. Use a vCluster or ask the operator to install it. With the dask Helm repository configured, run:

helm repo update
helm upgrade --install dask-gateway dask/dask-gateway \
  -n "${DEFAULT_NAMESPACE:-default}" \
  --create-namespace \
  --set gateway.auth.type=simple \
  --set gateway.auth.simple.password='' \
  --set traefik.service.type=ClusterIP \
  --set gateway.backend.image.name=ghcr.io/dask/dask-gateway \
  --set gateway.backend.image.tag=2025.4.0 \
  --wait --atomic

docs.title: MLflow
docs.text:
MLflow records experiment runs and their artifacts. This example stores its SQLite database on a PVC and artifacts in an existing S3 bucket. Set BUCKET to a bucket your Datalab can write to.

The PVC belongs to the current namespace. Check namespace deletion rules and the volume's reclaim policy before using it for records you need to keep. For a shared service, use a managed database and arrange artifact backups with the operator.

export BUCKET=ws-frank # replace accordingly

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: minio-creds
type: Opaque
stringData:
  accessKey: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
  secretKey: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: minio-config
data:
  endpoint: "${AWS_ENDPOINT_URL}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  selector:
    app: mlflow
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 5000
      targetPort: 5000
      protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mlflow
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mlflow
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: mlflow
          image: ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0
          command: ["/bin/sh","-lc"]
          args:
            - |
              python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip &&
              pip install --no-cache-dir boto3 &&
              exec mlflow server \
                --backend-store-uri sqlite:////mlflow/mlflow.db \
                --serve-artifacts \
                --artifacts-destination s3://"${BUCKET}"/mlruns \
                --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 \
                --workers 2 \
                --allowed-hosts '*' \
                --cors-allowed-origins '*'
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5000
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "300m", memory: "2Gi" }
          env:
            - name: MLFLOW_S3_ENDPOINT_URL
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef: { name: minio-config, key: endpoint }
            - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: accessKey }
            - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: secretKey }
            - name: AWS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE
              value: "true"
            - name: AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED
              value: "true"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /mlflow
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: mlflow
EOF
Open the MLflow interface through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/mlflow 5000:5000

Point your code at the forwarded tracking server:

export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI="http://127.0.0.1:5000"

docs.title: PostgreSQL with psql
docs.text:
If your Datalab provides database credentials through POSTGRES_<HOST>_<DATABASE>_URL_EXTERNAL environment variables, you can connect to the managed PostgreSQL instance by starting a Pod that opens a psql shell.

envsubst <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pgsql-debug
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: psql
    image: postgres:17
    stdin: true
    tty: true
    command:
      - sh
      - -lc
      - |
        exec psql "$POSTGRES_URL_EXTERNAL"
    env:
      - name: POSTGRES_URL_EXTERNAL
        value: ${POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL_EXTERNAL}
EOF

Attach to the Pod after it starts:

kubectl attach -it pgsql-debug

Use psql to create and query a test table:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
\l

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo;

CREATE TABLE demo (
    id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now(),
    meta jsonb
);

INSERT INTO demo (name, meta) VALUES
('alpha', '{"type":"test","value":1}'),
('beta',  '{"type":"test","value":2}'),
('gamma', '{"type":"prod","value":3}');

SELECT * FROM demo;

docs.title: Keep or remove a service
docs.text: Remove test services when the experiment ends. Before keeping one, agree with the platform team on its storage, backups, monitoring, upgrades, and deletion. Back up the service data separately from the session volume.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The platform ingress controller protects Datalab sessions. Configure sign-in and authorization before users start a session. The examples below use Kyverno policies to configure NGINX or APISIX session Ingress objects.

docs.title: Keycloak clients and roles
docs.text:
Users in spec.users must already exist in the realm selected by EnvironmentConfig.data.iam.realm. Provider Datalab creates a confidential client named after the Datalab, groups for its users and administrators, and their memberships and role mappings. The client disables implicit, device, and direct access grants. Role scope mappings limit the Datalab client roles included in its tokens.

Role Assigned to Used for ws_access Datalab users Browser access ws_admin Datalab administrators Browser access with the admin role ws_api The client service account Machine access through client credentials

The runtime Secret <datalab>-oauth2-client contains client_id and client_secret. Anyone who can read it can request a machine token for that Datalab. Give access only to users and services that need it.

A service can require extra token audiences. List them in EnvironmentConfig.data.iam.extraAudiences and use the same values in the service's token checks. The S3 endpoint adds the Datalab client ID as an audience when enabled. Other OAuth clients that call these services must emit the required audience and roles too.

docs.title: Apply ingress policy
docs.text:
Apply controller settings through platform policy so they cover every session Ingress. These examples use Kyverno CEL policies. Kyverno is needed only for these examples, not by Provider Datalab itself. Check that the installed Kyverno CRDs serve MutatingPolicy and GeneratingPolicy in policies.kyverno.io/v1.

For the other access controls, see Security.

docs.title: Generated session resources
docs.text:
For a Datalab named s-jane with a default session, set ingress.domain to lab.acme.org. Educates then creates session ingress hosts such as:

s-jane-default.lab.acme.org
editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.org
s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.org
data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.org
s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.org

The generated ingresses carry labels that are suitable for platform policy:

training.educates.dev/application: workshop
training.educates.dev/component: session
training.educates.dev/environment.name: s-jane

Provider Datalab also creates a confidential Keycloak client named after the Datalab. For s-jane, the generated client includes redirect and web-origin entries for the Datalab root and each declared session host:

https://s-jane.lab.acme.org/*
https://s-jane-default.lab.acme.org/*
https://editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.org/*
https://s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.org/*
https://data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.org/*
https://s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.org/*
http://localhost:*

A service that belongs to s-jane can use this client. Shared browser ingress can use a central platform client and check the generated Datalab roles.

To call a Datalab-owned service with a machine token, read client_id and client_secret from <datalab>-oauth2-client, request a token with grant_type=client_credentials, then send that access token to the service. Its policy should require ws_api and any configured audience.

docs.title: Set the shared ingress settings
docs.text:
Change ingress.class to match the ingress controller you operate.

apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1beta1
kind: EnvironmentConfig
metadata:
  name: datalab
data:
  iam:
    realm: acme
  ingress:
    class: apisix # use "nginx" for the nginx example
    domain: lab.acme.org
    secret: workspace-tls
  storage:
    endpoint: https://s3.acme.org
    provider: Other
    region: acme
    forcePathStyle: "true"
    secretNamespace: workspace
    type: s3

The Educates installation must use the same ingress class, domain, and TLS secret. For example, an APISIX-based deployment would set:

clusterIngressDomain: lab.acme.org
clusterIngressClass: apisix
tlsCertificateRef:
  name: workspace-tls
  namespace: workspace

For TLS, use a wildcard certificate for the session domain:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: workspace-cert
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  dnsNames:
  - "*.lab.acme.org"
  issuerRef:
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    name: letsencrypt-dns-prod
  secretName: workspace-tls

docs.title: NGINX Ingress with OAuth2 Proxy
docs.text:
Run OAuth2 Proxy as a shared service and add external-auth annotations to the session Ingress objects.

Give that proxy its own OAuth client with a redirect URI such as:

https://auth.lab.acme.org/oauth2/callback

The shared proxy can use one client for all Datalabs. Its authorization policy must still check access to the Datalab named in the requested host.

apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: MutatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: protect-workshop-sessions-nginx
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  evaluation:
    admission:
      enabled: true
    background:
      enabled: false
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [networking.k8s.io]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [ingresses]
  matchConditions:
    - name: is-workshop-session
      expression: >-
        has(object.metadata.labels) &&
        'training.educates.dev/application' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/application'] == 'workshop' &&
        'training.educates.dev/component' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/component'] == 'session'
    - name: uses-nginx
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.ingressClassName) &&
        object.spec.ingressClassName == 'nginx'
    - name: uses-datalab-domain
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.rules) && object.spec.rules.exists(rule,
          has(rule.host) && rule.host.endsWith('.lab.acme.org'))
  mutations:
    - patchType: ApplyConfiguration
      applyConfiguration:
        expression: |
          Object{
            metadata: Object.metadata{
              annotations: {
                "nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url": "https://auth.lab.acme.org/oauth2/auth",
                "nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin": "https://auth.lab.acme.org/oauth2/start?rd=https://$host$escaped_request_uri",
                "nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-response-headers": "Authorization,X-Auth-Request-User,X-Auth-Request-Email,X-Auth-Request-Preferred-Username"
              }
            }
          }

Set the proxy cookie domain to cover the session hosts, for example .lab.acme.org, and allow redirects only to that domain.

docs.title: APISIX Ingress configured by Kyverno
docs.text:
The Kyverno generating policy creates an ApisixPluginConfig in the session namespace. The mutating policy adds its name to the Ingress annotation. APISIX then uses that configuration for incoming requests. Kyverno configures the Ingress; it does not check browser tokens on each request.

The existing repository example uses openid-connect with a central client named datalab-sessions. It also contains an opa plugin entry that points to an external OPA service. The example does not deploy that service or supply its policy. Use that entry only with an OPA service configured by your platform. Provider Datalab itself does not require OPA.

Kyverno needs permission to create ApisixPluginConfig resources in the generated session namespaces:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: kyverno:datalab-session-apisix-pluginconfigs
  labels:
    rbac.kyverno.io/aggregate-to-admission-controller: "true"
    rbac.kyverno.io/aggregate-to-background-controller: "true"
rules:
- apiGroups:
  - apisix.apache.org
  resources:
  - apisixpluginconfigs
  verbs:
  - get
  - list
  - watch
  - create
  - update
  - patch
  - delete

The Kyverno policies below do not need Secret read access because they use a central public OAuth client. If your platform uses a confidential central client, inject that platform-managed credential with the ingress controller's supported Secret mechanism instead of the generated per-Datalab runtime Secret.

The CEL policies generate one APISIX plugin config per session namespace and annotate the matching workshop ingress to use it:

apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: GeneratingPolicy
metadata:
  name: generate-workshop-session-apisix-pluginconfigs
spec:
  evaluation:
    synchronize:
      enabled: false
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [networking.k8s.io]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [ingresses]
  matchConditions:
    - name: is-workshop-session
      expression: >-
        has(object.metadata.labels) &&
        'training.educates.dev/application' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/application'] == 'workshop' &&
        'training.educates.dev/component' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/component'] == 'session'
    - name: uses-apisix
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.ingressClassName) &&
        object.spec.ingressClassName == 'apisix'
    - name: uses-datalab-domain
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.rules) && object.spec.rules.exists(rule,
          has(rule.host) && rule.host.endsWith('.lab.acme.org'))
    - name: has-datalab-name
      expression: >-
        'training.educates.dev/environment.name' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/environment.name'] != ''
  variables:
    - name: environmentName
      expression: object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/environment.name']
    - name: targetNamespace
      expression: object.metadata.namespace
  generate:
    - template:
        interpolate: cel
        value: |
          apiVersion: apisix.apache.org/v2
          kind: ApisixPluginConfig
          metadata:
            name: datalab-session-oidc-(( variables.environmentName ))
            namespace: (( variables.targetNamespace ))
            labels:
              training.educates.dev/application: workshop
              training.educates.dev/component: session
              training.educates.dev/environment.name: (( variables.environmentName ))
          spec:
            plugins:
              - name: openid-connect
                enable: true
                config:
                  discovery: "https://iam-auth.acme.org/realms/acme/.well-known/openid-configuration"
                  use_jwks: true
                  bearer_only: false
                  scope: openid profile email roles
                  client_id: datalab-sessions
                  client_secret: ""
                  session:
                    secret: (( random.random('[A-Za-z0-9]{32}') ))
                  access_token_in_authorization_header: true
                  set_access_token_header: true
                  set_id_token_header: false
                  set_userinfo_header: false
                  set_refresh_token_header: false
              - name: opa
                enable: true
                config:
                  host: http://opa.iam:8181
                  policy: example/datalab/session
---
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: MutatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: annotate-workshop-sessions-for-apisix
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  evaluation:
    admission:
      enabled: true
    background:
      enabled: false
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [networking.k8s.io]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [ingresses]
  matchConditions:
    - name: is-workshop-session
      expression: >-
        has(object.metadata.labels) &&
        'training.educates.dev/application' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/application'] == 'workshop' &&
        'training.educates.dev/component' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/component'] == 'session'
    - name: uses-apisix
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.ingressClassName) &&
        object.spec.ingressClassName == 'apisix'
    - name: uses-datalab-domain
      expression: >-
        has(object.spec.rules) && object.spec.rules.exists(rule,
          has(rule.host) && rule.host.endsWith('.lab.acme.org'))
    - name: has-datalab-name
      expression: >-
        'training.educates.dev/environment.name' in object.metadata.labels &&
        object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/environment.name'] != ''
  variables:
    - name: environmentName
      expression: object.metadata.labels['training.educates.dev/environment.name']
  mutations:
    - patchType: ApplyConfiguration
      applyConfiguration:
        expression: |
          Object{
            metadata: Object.metadata{
              annotations: {
                "k8s.apisix.apache.org/plugin-config-name":
                  "datalab-session-oidc-" + variables.environmentName
              }
            }
          }

The external authorizer in this example must check access to the requested Datalab. Its endpoint and policy path are placeholders for the platform's settings.

The session secret is generated when Kyverno creates the ApisixPluginConfig. Disabled synchronization keeps the generated object stable. If you change the plugin template for an existing session, recreate the generated plugin config or restart the session so Kyverno can generate a new one.

This example forwards the access token in the Authorization header and disables ID token, userinfo, and refresh token forwarding. Check that those settings match the authorization plugins and upstream service you use.

For another ingress controller, match the session Ingress objects by label and domain, then attach its authentication and authorization settings.

The complete manifests are in the repository:

  • NGINX and OAuth2 Proxy
  • APISIX Kyverno policies

docs.title: Install Provider Datalab
docs.text: This guide prepares the platform, installs the configuration package, and creates a first Datalab. Run the commands with access to the target cluster. Use your platform's GitOps and Secret tools for a shared installation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The cluster needs Crossplane, Educates, an ingress controller, Keycloak, and an S3-compatible object store. The CNI must enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Use Crossplane from the supported range in the package's metadata.

Install Educates with its CRDs and controller RBAC before creating Datalabs. Follow the Educates installation guide. The Educates ingress class, domain, and TLS Secret must match the settings below.

Install the operators for the managed stores you plan to offer:

Datalab field Operator Required resource API spec.databases Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator PostgresCluster in postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/v1 spec.documentStores MongoDB Kubernetes Operator MongoDBCommunity in mongodbcommunity.mongodb.com/v1 spec.cacheStores Redis Kubernetes Operator Redis in redis.redis.opstreelabs.in/v1beta2 spec.vectorStores Qdrant Operator QdrantCluster in qdrant.io/v1alpha1

Check the served APIs and fields before upgrading an operator. The integration tests contain the dependency settings used by this repository. Configure storage, backup and restore, monitoring, and deletion for each store you offer.

Gateway exposure also needs a Gateway API controller. Data uses HTTPRoute with HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners. External PostgreSQL access uses TLSRoute in gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 and direct TLS with SNI.

docs.title: 1. Choose the claim namespace
docs.text:
This guide uses workspace for Datalab resources and their namespaced ProviderConfigs:

kubectl create namespace workspace

The input storage Secret lives in storage.secretNamespace, set below. This guide also uses workspace for that namespace. Educates creates the runtime namespaces when the Datalab is reconciled.

docs.title: 2. Install provider dependencies
docs.text:
Apply the files in educates/dependencies/ in this order:

File Purpose 00-mrap.yaml Activate the managed resource kinds used by the composition. 01-deploymentRuntimeConfigs.yaml Set provider and function Pod security. 02-providers.yaml Install the Kubernetes, Helm, and Keycloak providers. 03-providerConfigs.yaml Configure those providers in the claim namespace. functions.yaml Install the composition functions. rbac.yaml Grant provider-kubernetes access to the resources it manages.

Apply 03-providerConfigs.yaml with kubectl apply -n workspace -f .... Create its referenced Keycloak credential Secret in that namespace through your platform's Secret tools. The Keycloak account needs permission to manage clients, service-account roles, groups, memberships, and role mappings in the target realm.

Use the package pins in the dependency manifests. Wait for the provider and function revisions to report healthy before installing the configuration package. The provider-kubernetes RBAC includes access to Pods for readiness checks and PVCs for session storage.

docs.title: 3. Install the configuration package
docs.text:
Save this resource as configuration.yaml. Replace 0.11.0-rc.2 with the release tag you want to install.

apiVersion: pkg.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Configuration
metadata:
  name: datalab-educates
spec:
  package: ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-datalab/educates:0.11.0-rc.2
  skipDependencyResolution: true

Apply it and check the package conditions:

kubectl apply -f configuration.yaml
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io

The package installs the Datalab resource definition and composition. Its providers and functions are managed separately by the platform.

docs.title: 4. Set the shared environment
docs.text:
Create an EnvironmentConfig named datalab with values for your cluster. This example uses a permanent Data Ingress:

apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1beta1
kind: EnvironmentConfig
metadata:
  name: datalab
data:
  iam:
    realm: demo
    issuerURL: https://identity.example.org/realms/demo
    internalURL: http://keycloak.keycloak:8080/realms/demo
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    class: nginx
    domain: lab.example.org
    secret: wildcard-tls
    annotations: {}
  storage:
    endpoint: https://s3.example.org
    provider: Other
    region: us-east-1
    forcePathStyle: "true"
    secretNamespace: workspace
    type: s3
  storageClasses:
    allowed:
    - sbs-default
    - sbs-default-retain
  network:
    externalEgressCIDRs:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
    - ::/0
    serviceCIDR: "10.43.0.0/16"
    podCIDRs:
    - 10.42.0.0/16
    blacklistIPs:
    - 169.254.169.254/32
    - fd00:ec2::254/128
    - 169.254.42.42/32
    - fd00:42::42/128
    excludePolicies: []
  defaults:
    overallQuota:
      storage: 100Gi
    security:
      externalEgress: true

Replace the example storage classes, network ranges, and DNS names before applying it. To select another EnvironmentConfig for one Datalab, set its datalabs.pkg.internal/environment annotation or label to that config's name.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Set iam.realm to the Keycloak realm that contains your users. The public iam.issuerURL is used for browser login; iam.internalURL is used for in-cluster token and signing-key requests. The IAM namespace defaults to keycloak. Set iam.namespace if your installation uses another namespace.

Provider Datalab creates a confidential OAuth client, groups, roles, and memberships for each Datalab. Platform ingress policy must protect session access. See Authentication for the role model and the controller examples.

docs.title: Data address
docs.text:
ingress.enabled and httpRoute.enabled both default to false. In that case, a session reaches Data through its Educates-authenticated ingress. Enable one setting to give each Datalab a permanent Data address. Enabling both stops reconciliation.

Both options need iam.issuerURL, iam.internalURL, and ingress.domain. An Ingress also needs ingress.class and ingress.secret. Use ingress.annotations for controller settings.

For Gateway API exposure, merge this block into the EnvironmentConfig:

data:
  ingress:
    enabled: false
    class: nginx
    domain: lab.example.org
    secret: wildcard-tls
  httpRoute:
    enabled: true
    enableS3: false
    parentName: default
    parentNamespace: gateway-system
    sectionName: workspaces-https
    httpSectionName: workspaces-http

The Gateway needs HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners and must accept routes from Datalab runtime namespaces. It manages the permanent Data certificate. Keep ingress.class and ingress.secret for Educates session Ingress objects.

Set httpRoute.enableS3: true to add the experimental read-only S3 endpoint for every Data-enabled Datalab in the environment. Browser and S3 requests then use the same hostname. See S3 client access for the controller requirements and client setup.

docs.title: Public catalog CORS
docs.text: packageR allows all browser origins (*) for public catalog access. No chart or EnvironmentConfig CORS setting is needed. To restrict origins, configure the Gateway to replace or remove backend CORS headers and handle preflight requests. Adding another CORS header does not restrict the wildcard. Check the controller's support for HTTPRoute CORS filters. Cookie-based cross-origin access needs its own policy.

docs.title: Storage and quotas
docs.text:
storage.endpoint is the S3 address used by session tools and packageR. It must be reachable from the runtime Pods. Browsers connect to Data rather than directly to object storage. Use storage.forcePathStyle when the store requires path-style addresses.

storageClasses.allowed restricts the classes used by session PVCs. A requested class is used when listed; otherwise the first listed class is used. With an empty or omitted list, any requested class is allowed.

defaults.overallQuota.storage sets the total PVC request limit for each Datalab environment namespace. A Datalab can override it with spec.overallQuota.storage. If neither is set, the limit is 100Gi. PVCs in other namespaces are outside that quota.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Set network.podCIDRs and network.serviceCIDR to the host cluster's network ranges. They are excluded from broad external egress so that it does not also allow access to other Datalab namespaces. Use the cluster configuration for the Service CIDR. A DNS Service IP alone does not identify the full range. Pod CIDRs can be listed with:

kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDR}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDRs}{"\n"}{end}'

network.externalEgressCIDRs lists the external ranges allowed when externalEgress is true. Use 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 for all external IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, or list narrower ranges. An empty list grants no broad external access. network.blacklistIPs excludes ranges such as cloud metadata endpoints from that rule.

For a backend Pod in another namespace, add an internalEgress entry:

network:
  internalEgress:
  - namespace: minio
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        v1.min.io/tenant: default
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000

Data uses these rules to reach object storage. The Data and S3 proxies also have an IAM egress rule for TCP port 8080 in the configured IAM namespace. When replacing a manual IAM policy, verify the composed policy and an S3 read before removal, then repeat the read without the manual policy.

Use network.excludePolicies only when another policy system supplies the same controls. See Network policies for the generated policies and how they combine.

docs.title: 5. Supply storage credentials
docs.text:
Create the object-storage bucket and credentials through your platform's storage process or Provider Storage. Provider Datalab reads an existing input Secret. Its name comes from spec.secretName, or the Datalab name when that field is omitted.

The Secret must exist in storage.secretNamespace and contain AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. The storage identity must permit bucket listing with s3:ListAllMyBuckets. The endpoint must support path-style S3 requests.

For a manual setup, create the Secret with your credential values:

kubectl -n workspace create secret generic demo \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<KEY_ID> \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<SECRET>

Use the platform's Secret tools for shared installations. Keep live credentials out of Git.

docs.title: 6. Create a Datalab
docs.text:
Save this resource as datalab.yaml. Alice must already exist in Keycloak.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: demo
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users:
  - alice
  sessions:
  - name: default

Apply it and check its conditions:

kubectl apply -f datalab.yaml
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab demo -n workspace

The default session starts and gets a workspace PVC. Its Data tab opens the shared file browser. With the permanent address enabled, users can also open Data without a session and publish files through the default public share. See Use a Datalab for session state, managed services, workshop files, and sharing.

docs.title: 7. Check the installation
docs.text:
Check that provider and function revisions are healthy and that the Datalab reports Synced=True and Ready=True:

kubectl get providers.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get providerrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functionrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace

If reconciliation fails, read the Datalab conditions and events. Check that the required APIs are served. The provider APIs used here are namespaced:

kubectl api-resources --api-group=kubernetes.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=helm.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=keycloak.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=gateway.networking.k8s.io

For a managed store, also check its API group from the prerequisite table. Then verify the session login, Data address, storage access, and each requested service before giving the Datalab to users.

docs.title: S3 client access
docs.text: The read-only S3 endpoint is experimental. Range reads currently return HTTP 200 with Content-Range, rather than HTTP 206.

docs.title: Enable the endpoint
docs.text:
Set EnvironmentConfig.data.httpRoute.enableS3: true to add a read-only S3 endpoint on the shared Data hostname for every Data-enabled Datalab in the environment. There is no per-Datalab override. Set httpRoute.enabled: true and ingress.enabled: false. Use a Gateway API controller that supports HTTPRoute header regular expressions, such as Contour, with HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners for the Data hostnames. Add a ReferenceGrant if the Gateway uses a certificate Secret from another namespace.

Merge these settings into the selected EnvironmentConfig:

data:
  ingress:
    enabled: false
    domain: lab.acme.com
  httpRoute:
    enabled: true
    enableS3: true
    parentName: default
    parentNamespace: gateway-system
    sectionName: workspaces-https
    httpSectionName: workspaces-http

With enableS3: false or omitted, the same HTTPRoutes serve only the browser endpoint. The controller does not create an S3 service or S3 routing rule.

Allow the runtime to reach object storage through the environment's network settings. The composed S3 policy permits IAM traffic on TCP port 8080 in the configured IAM namespace. The Gateway must be able to reach the S3 service. See Network access for the shared settings.

docs.title: S3 access to s-joe
docs.text:
The Joe example creates the Datalab s-joe and selects datalab-custom. With the example EnvironmentConfig, its endpoint is https://s-joe.lab.acme.com and its issuer is https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme. Replace these example DNS names with your environment's values.

Keycloak checks CLIENT_SECRET and issues a JWT. The AWS CLI sends it as AWS_SESSION_TOKEN in the X-Amz-Security-Token header. NGINX checks the tenant ID and passes the token to oauth2-proxy, which checks its signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and Datalab role. After authorization, rclone serve s3 checks the original AWS SigV4 request using s-joe as both signing values. It serves read-only data through separate upstream storage credentials.

AWS CLI
  │ HTTPS :443 → s-joe.lab.acme.com
  ▼
Contour / Envoy
  │ HTTP → Service data-s3 :8080
  ▼
NGINX gateway :8080
  ├─ Auth subrequest → oauth2-proxy 127.0.0.1:4180
  │                     └─ Fetch signing keys → Keycloak
  │                        (example internal URL: keycloak.keycloak:8080)
  │
  └─ If authorized → rclone 127.0.0.1:8081
                         └─ HTTPS → upstream S3 storage (s3.acme :443)

NGINX, oauth2-proxy, and rclone share the data-s3 Pod and use localhost for calls within that Pod. The Gateway implementation and upstream storage depend on your environment. The example internal Keycloak URL uses Service port 8080; other installations can use a different Service port.

Credential field Value AccessKeyId s-joe SecretAccessKey s-joe SessionToken Keycloak JWT access token Expiration Token expiry

The signing values are public tenant identifiers. They do not grant access without a valid JWT. The token must include s-joe in aud and at least one of ws_access, ws_admin, or ws_api under resource_access.s-joe.roles. These are Keycloak client roles, separate from OAuth scopes. All three permit reads. The upstream storage policy limits which buckets and objects the Datalab can read. Missing or invalid tokens cannot use a browser cookie or an unsigned request as a fallback.

The generated Datalab client adds its own audience when S3 is enabled. Other OAuth clients must emit the same audience and tenant roles. Service-account tokens do not need a verified email address.

The following Bash commands use the credential helper from the repository root. It uses the client credentials grant with s-joe as the client ID. At the prompt, enter the client_secret from the generated s-joe-oauth2-client Secret in the runtime namespace. Replace example-data with a bucket that the Datalab can read. Both methods use path-style requests.

docs.title: Manual token retrieval
docs.text:
if [ -z "${CLIENT_SECRET:-}" ]; then
  CLIENT_SECRET="$(python3 -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("CLIENT_SECRET: "))')"
fi
export CLIENT_SECRET
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s-joe AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=s-joe
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://s-joe.lab.acme.com
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_PROFILE=s-joe
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-joe

credentials="$(python3 tests/s3/s3-credentials.py \
  --tenant s-joe \
  --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme)"
AWS_SESSION_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$credentials" | \
  python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["SessionToken"])')"
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset credentials

aws s3 ls s3://example-data/

Run the token retrieval command again after the token expires, or use automatic renewal below.

docs.title: Automatic token renewal with credential_process
docs.text:
Clear the manual AWS settings so that the CLI uses the profile's credential process. The CLI obtains new credentials when needed, using the helper's Expiration value.

unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset AWS_CONFIG_FILE AWS_PROFILE AWS_ENDPOINT_URL
unset AWS_DEFAULT_REGION AWS_REGION

if [ -z "${CLIENT_SECRET:-}" ]; then
  CLIENT_SECRET="$(python3 -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("CLIENT_SECRET: "))')"
fi
export CLIENT_SECRET
export AWS_PROFILE=s-joe

aws configure set region us-east-1 --profile s-joe
aws configure set endpoint_url https://s-joe.lab.acme.com --profile s-joe
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-joe
aws configure set credential_process \
  "python3 \"$PWD/tests/s3/s3-credentials.py\" --tenant s-joe --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme" \
  --profile s-joe

aws s3 ls s3://example-data/

Keep CLIENT_SECRET available in the environment of the AWS CLI or SDK process. If you move the repository, update the helper's absolute path in the profile.

The endpoint supports list, HEAD, GET, and byte-range GET requests. It remains read only when spec.data.readOnlyMount is false. Writes and presigned S3 URLs are rejected. packageR download and share links use the browser route.

docs.title: Use a Datalab
docs.text: A Datalab resource defines the users, sessions, and services for a team. The operator supplies the shared storage, identity, and network settings. Complete installation before applying these examples.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session is a named workspace with an editor, terminal, and persistent home directory. Declare the sessions you need in spec.sessions:

spec:
  sessions:
  - name: default
  - name: analysis
    state: stopped

The state defaults to started. A started session has an Educates WorkshopSession and a workspace Pod. A stopped session keeps its PVC without a running workspace. Change its state to started to use the same PVC again. Several sessions can run at once; each has its own Pod and PVC and shares the Datalab's credentials and managed services.

With no declared sessions, the Datalab still creates its shared services. It creates no session Pods or workspace PVCs.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Each declared session has a PVC mounted at /home/eduk8s. Set its size and StorageClass with:

spec:
  quota:
    storage: 20Gi
  persistence:
    storageClassName: sbs-default

The operator can restrict classes through EnvironmentConfig.data.storageClasses.allowed. A requested class must be in that list; otherwise the first listed class is used. With no list, Kubernetes uses the requested class or the cluster default.

Use the session volume for code, libraries, and workspace files. Keep datasets in object storage and database records in a managed database. Arrange backups and recovery with the operator. Test session stop, start, and recovery with your platform's storage before relying on them.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Use spec.databases to request a PostgreSQL cluster and its logical databases:

spec:
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - dev
      - prod
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

This creates the pg0 cluster with dev and prod databases. The PostgreSQL operator manages the database Pods, credentials, and configured backups. Stopping a session does not stop the database.

Sessions receive connection settings such as POSTGRES_PG0_HOST, POSTGRES_PG0_PORT, and POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The generated <datalab>-datalab Secret holds these values. When the platform enables an external TLSRoute, it also supplies POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL_EXTERNAL. External connections require a client that supports direct TLS with SNI.

docs.title: Document, cache, and vector stores
docs.text:
Use these fields to request MongoDB, Redis, and Qdrant stores:

spec:
  documentStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
  cacheStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
  vectorStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi

Each store needs its operator installed in the cluster. For the name prod, sessions receive MONGO_PROD_URI, REDIS_PROD_URL, and QDRANT_PROD_URL, along with separate host and credential fields where available.

The composition creates <store>-mongodb-auth, <store>-redis-auth, and <store>-qdrant-auth Secrets. It watches their values and copies connection settings into <datalab>-datalab. Sessions import those settings as environment variables. Restart a session to load changed values.

docs.title: Docker registry
docs.text:
Use spec.registry to add a registry to the session:

spec:
  registry:
    enabled: true
    storage: 3Gi

Use it to push and pull images within the Datalab. Agree with the operator on retention, scanning, and backups if you need to keep the images.

docs.title: Data and sharing
docs.text:
The Data service, packageR, is a file browser for the Datalab's object storage. It is enabled by default. A session's Data tab opens this shared service. When the operator enables a permanent Data address, you can use it without a running session.

The file browser requires sign-in. You can share individual files through temporary download URLs, or folders through public share links. Recipients do not need a Datalab account.

Set spec.data.enabled: false when creating a Datalab to omit the service and its Data tabs. This setting cannot change after creation. Set spec.data.readOnlyMount: true for read-only application permissions. Storage IAM still limits every request.

docs.title: Sharing data with the world
docs.text:
Put files in <datalab>/public in the bucket named after your Datalab, then send the public share link. For example, s-jane/public/results.csv belongs to the default public share for s-jane. A folder named public elsewhere is not shared automatically.

Public sharing needs a permanent Data address. Upload files through the Data browser when write access is allowed, or use your storage tools. Anyone with the link can browse and download those files without signing in.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The operator protects session ingress and checks access against the generated Datalab roles. Users in spec.users must exist in the configured Keycloak realm. See Authentication for the client and role model and the NGINX and APISIX setup examples.

docs.title: Files and the Workshop tab
docs.text:
Use spec.files to load workshop content from Git, an OCI image, or an HTTP archive. For example:

spec:
  files:
  - git:
      url: https://github.com/versioneer-tech/datalab-example
      ref: origin/main
    includePaths:
    - /workshop/**
    path: .

Adding a source enables the Workshop tab. With no sources, the tab is hidden. Use includePaths, excludePaths, newRootPath, and path to select and place the files.

docs.title: vCluster
docs.text: Set spec.vcluster: true to give each started session a virtual Kubernetes API. With false, workloads use the host cluster namespace directly. The virtual API does not isolate Pods from the host. The host's network and Pod security rules still apply.

docs.title: Storage Secret
docs.text:
A Datalab needs credentials for an existing S3-compatible store. Set spec.secretName to the input Secret name. If omitted, the Datalab name is used. The operator sets its namespace with EnvironmentConfig.data.storage.secretNamespace and the endpoint with EnvironmentConfig.data.storage.endpoint.

The Secret must contain AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. The Data service needs network access to that endpoint. Browsers connect to Data rather than directly to storage.

docs.title: Security and access policy
docs.text:
Use spec.security to set session privileges and access:

Field Effect policy Selects restricted, baseline, or privileged Pod security. Privileged mode enables Docker with local storage. kubernetesAccess Controls whether the session gets a Kubernetes service account token. kubernetesRole Selects view, edit, or admin access. externalEgress Controls external network access through the generated policies.

The operator sets shared defaults in EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.security. Data uses the same egress rules to reach object storage. See Network policies for the policy rules and Session access for what a session can use.

docs.title: Resource quotas
docs.text:
Use spec.quota for session limits and spec.overallQuota for the total PVC requests in the Datalab environment namespace:

spec:
  quota:
    memory: 4Gi
    storage: 20Gi
    budget: large
  overallQuota:
    storage: 100Gi

Session defaults are 2Gi memory, 1Gi storage, and the medium Educates budget. The operator can change them through EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.quota.

The total storage quota defaults to 100Gi, or EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.overallQuota.storage when set. It covers PVC requests in the environment namespace, not PVCs in other namespaces.

docs.title: S3 client access
docs.text: The optional S3 endpoint lets AWS tools read Datalab data through the same host as the Data browser. It is experimental and read only. The operator enables it for the environment. See S3 client access for setup, token handling, and AWS CLI examples.

docs.title: Identity and Keycloak resources
docs.text: Provider Datalab creates the client, groups, roles, and memberships for each Datalab. Human users get ws_access or ws_admin; the client service account gets ws_api. See Keycloak clients and roles for how services use them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: These examples use the manifests in examples/base/. The named users must exist in Keycloak and their input storage Secrets must exist before you apply the resources. Apply them in your claim namespace.

docs.title: Joe: Data without a session
docs.text:
Joe uses the shared Data service without starting a workspace. He can add a named session later.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  annotations:
    datalabs.pkg.internal/environment: datalab-custom
spec:
  users:
  - joe
  secretName: s-joe

docs.title: Jeff, Jim, and Jane: shared stores
docs.text:
This Datalab requests PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, and Qdrant stores. It starts no session and disables Data, Kubernetes API access, and external egress.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-jeff
spec:
  users:
    - jeff
    - jim
    - jane
  userOverrides:
    jim:
      grantedAt: "2025-01-10T19:00:00Z"
      role: admin
  secretName: s-jeff
  sessions: []
  vcluster: false
  data:
    enabled: false
  quota:
    memory: 6Gi
    storage: 1Gi
    budget: x-large
  files: []
  security:
    kubernetesAccess: false
    externalEgress: false
  registry:
    enabled: false
  documentStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
  cacheStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
  vectorStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - dev
      - prod
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

docs.title: Jane: a privileged workspace
docs.text:
Jane starts a session with a virtual Kubernetes API, the admin role, a registry, and a PostgreSQL database. Data is read only. Use this setup only when the operator has approved privileged workloads.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-jane
spec:
  users:
    - jane

John starts a default session and keeps an analysis session stopped. Workshop files come from Git, which enables the Workshop tab.

docs.title: Verifying provisioning
docs.text:
Check the Datalab conditions after applying a resource:

kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab s-jeff -n workspace

Synced=True means the composition reconciled. Ready=True means its resources report ready. Read the conditions and events if either is false.

docs.title: Find the storage Secret
docs.text:
Check that the referenced Secret exists in storage.secretNamespace:

kubectl get secret s-jeff -n workspace

Use your platform's credential tools to inspect or rotate its values.

docs.title: Connect to databases
docs.text:
Use the connection variables supplied to the session, such as POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The PostgreSQL operator also creates user Secrets named *-pguser-*. Use the database role assigned to your task; the postgres role has administrative access.

See Additional services for a psql example.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
A session can use the credentials, volumes, Kubernetes permissions, and network access available to its Pod. The platform operator decides which users may start sessions and which resources they may use.

Provider Datalab passes session security settings to Educates and creates network policies. Educates creates the workspace Pods and applies the namespace, role, and token settings. The cluster must enforce them through its CNI, admission rules, Pod security, and RBAC.

docs.title: Access to a Datalab
docs.text:
The ingress controller must handle session sign-in and authorization. Provider Datalab creates Keycloak clients, groups, and roles for each Datalab. Users receive ws_access or ws_admin; the client service account receives ws_api for machine access.

Shared browser ingress can use one platform OAuth client and check the Datalab roles for each requested host. Services belonging to one Datalab can use its generated client. See Authentication for the client model and controller examples.

Anyone who can read the runtime <datalab>-oauth2-client Secret can request machine tokens for that Datalab. Limit Secret access to the users and services that need it, and rotate credentials when access changes.

Public Data shares allow browsing and downloads without sign-in. Users should place only files they intend to publish in the Datalab's public folder. See Public sharing.

docs.title: Session defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Effect spec.security.policy baseline Selects the Educates namespace security policy. privileged also enables Docker. spec.security.kubernetesAccess true Makes a Kubernetes service account token available to the session. spec.security.kubernetesRole edit Sets the session's Kubernetes permissions. spec.security.externalEgress true Enables the external egress rule for the configured CIDRs. spec.vcluster false Uses the host namespace directly. When enabled, adds a virtual Kubernetes API.

Set shared security defaults in EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.security. Use stricter values when workspace code does not need Kubernetes access, external traffic, or privileged containers. A vCluster changes the Kubernetes API available to users; its Pods still run on the host cluster.

docs.title: Platform responsibilities
docs.text:
The platform team manages ingress authentication, the CNI, admission rules, RBAC, DNS, storage classes, quotas, and node access. It also manages cloud IAM, bucket policy, backup, retention, and audit for the data and services available to a Datalab.

NetworkPolicy rules are additive. Another policy can allow traffic that the generated policies do not allow. Standard NetworkPolicy also cannot express ordered deny rules or domain-name allowlists. Check the combined rules in the deployed cluster.

Privileged containers, host mounts, runtime sockets, and broad credentials can give workspace code access beyond its namespace. Approve those settings only for users and workloads that need them. Replacing a Pod or tightening a network rule does not revoke a leaked credential; rotate or revoke it at its source.

Session access describes what workspace code can use. Network policies lists the generated policies and the settings that control them.

docs.title: Network policies
docs.text: Provider Datalab creates egress policies through the Educates environment and Data policies directly in the runtime namespace. The cluster CNI must enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for these rules to take effect.

docs.title: Session security
docs.text:
Provider Datalab passes these fields to Educates:

Datalab field Educates setting spec.security.policy Namespace security policy spec.security.kubernetesAccess Kubernetes token enabled or disabled spec.security.kubernetesRole Namespace or vCluster role

The privileged policy also enables the Docker application with local storage. Educates applies these settings when it creates session resources.

docs.title: Generated egress policies
docs.text:
Policy Created when Allows deny-egress By default No egress by itself; other policies can allow traffic. allow-namespace-egress By default Traffic to Pods in the same runtime namespace. allow-dns-egress External egress, Data, or vCluster is enabled DNS to kube-system on TCP and UDP port 53. allow-vcluster-egress vCluster is enabled TCP ports 443 and 8443 to the same Datalab's vCluster control-plane Pods. allow-external-egress External egress is enabled The configured external CIDRs, minus excluded ranges. allow-internal-egress Internal targets are configured The selected backend Pods and ports in other namespaces.

The DNS rule lets Data resolve storage hosts and lets sessions resolve their vCluster Service. Namespace and Pod selectors on the vCluster rule limit it to the same Datalab.

NetworkPolicies are additive. deny-egress selects Pods for egress isolation; it does not override an allow rule in another selected policy. Check all policies that select a Pod when testing access.

docs.title: External and internal ranges
docs.text:
spec.security.externalEgress falls back to EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.security.externalEgress, then to true. The external allow rule uses these EnvironmentConfig fields:

Field under data.network Purpose externalEgressCIDRs External destination ranges. An empty list grants no broad external access. blacklistIPs Ranges excluded from that rule, such as cloud metadata endpoints. podCIDRs Host Pod networks excluded from broad external access. serviceCIDR Host Service network excluded from broad external access.

Use 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 to allow all external IPv4 and IPv6 destinations, or list narrower ranges. Supply the actual host cluster ranges so that this rule does not also grant access to other Datalab namespaces.

With externalEgress: false, the broad external rule is omitted. Same-namespace traffic, DNS needed by Data or a vCluster, and access to the Datalab's vCluster API remain allowed. Add internalEgress entries for required backends in other namespaces. Each entry selects a namespace, Pods, and destination ports. See Network access for an example.

docs.title: Data service policies
docs.text:
For session access, packageR accepts port 8888 from Educates workshop Pods. For permanent access, its OAuth proxy accepts port 4180. The file browser requires sign-in; public shares permit browsing and downloads without it.

The S3 service accepts Gateway traffic on port 8080. Data and S3 proxies can reach IAM on TCP port 8080 in the configured IAM namespace. Object-storage access follows the Datalab's egress rules.

docs.title: Replace or exclude policies
docs.text:
Use EnvironmentConfig.data.network.excludePolicies only when another policy system provides the required controls. Excluding allow-dns-egress also suppresses the Data DNS policy.

Before changing these settings, verify the CNI, the allowed network ranges, and every required cross-namespace connection. Restrict who can change NetworkPolicies or request privileged and admin settings through the platform's RBAC and admission policy.

docs.title: Session access
docs.text: A Datalab session runs as a Pod in the host cluster. Its access comes from Kubernetes permissions, credentials, volumes, and network rules. Check these together when deciding which code a user may run.

docs.title: What a session can use
docs.text:
The session can read and write the data allowed by its storage and service credentials. It can use the mounted workspace PVC and any other volumes made available to the Pod. Docker, registries, host mounts, or runtime sockets can add further access.

spec.security.kubernetesAccess controls whether the session gets a Kubernetes token. spec.security.kubernetesRole sets its role. With spec.vcluster: false, workloads use the host namespace directly. With true, the session gets a virtual Kubernetes API, while its workloads still run on host Pods under the host's security and network rules.

spec.security.policy selects restricted, baseline, or privileged. Privileged mode enables Docker. The operator decides who may enable it.

A user or service that can read <datalab>-oauth2-client in the runtime namespace can request machine tokens. Those tokens carry ws_api. Browser access uses the separate ws_access and ws_admin roles.

docs.title: Example settings
docs.text:
Example Settings Access s-jeff No session, Data disabled, Kubernetes access disabled Managed stores run without a workspace. A session added later can use the supplied service credentials. s-joe and s-john Host namespace, baseline policy, default edit role Session code can use its Kubernetes token unless the operator changes the default. s-jane vCluster, privileged policy, admin role, registry enabled Session code has broad permissions. Use only with operator approval.

The manifests are in examples/base/. Their settings are examples, not a required policy for other Datalabs.

docs.title: Explain access to users
docs.text:
Before users start a session, tell them which data and services it can use, whether Kubernetes and internet access are available, and whether Docker or privileged workloads are allowed. Explain what survives a stop or deletion, what is backed up, and who can restore it.

See Security for the platform's responsibilities and Network policies for egress rules.
